title: BJP Lost the Gokul Dairy Vote. A Cabinet Rule Change Reopened the Fight for Control
excerpt: Satej Patil's panel won Maharashtra's largest milk cooperative 13-12. The cabinet then approved government-nominated voting members — and the opposition calls it a stolen mandate.
body:
• Congress MLC Satej Patil's panel won the Kolhapur Gokul dairy election 13 seats to the ruling Mahayuti's 12, taking control of Maharashtra's largest milk cooperative.
  • Days later, the state cabinet approved appointing five government-nominated members to cooperative managing committees, four of them with voting rights — a move the opposition says overturns the verdict.
  • Rahul Gandhi accused the BJP of changing the rules after losing; NCP (SP) leader Rohit Pawar urged people to gather outside Gokul's offices, and a leader of the ruling Shiv Sena also criticised the move.
  • Gokul collects milk from more than 8,000 village societies and turns over roughly Rs 4,000 crore a year — which is why a dairy board election carries state-level political weight.

The BJP-led Mahayuti lost the election. Then the rules changed. That sequence — a narrow defeat at Maharashtra's largest dairy cooperative followed by a cabinet decision that could still deliver control — has turned a Kolhapur milk union poll into a state political fight, with Rahul Gandhi accusing the BJP of stealing a mandate it failed to win.

The election the ruling alliance lost

In the election to the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union — the cooperative known by its brand name, Gokul — the Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samavichari Aghadi backed by Congress MLC Satej Patil won 13 of the 25 board seats, against 12 for the Mahayuti, according to EDairy News' report sourced to The Indian Express. Turnout was near total: 5,416 of 5,418 accredited delegates from primary dairy societies voted across 35 polling stations. The Mahayuti had campaigned with two cabinet ministers, ten MLAs and two MPs; its defeat also ended the board tenure of Navid Mushrif, whose father, cabinet minister Hasan Mushrif, has alleged a conspiracy behind the result.

The cabinet decision that followed

On Wednesday, the Maharashtra cabinet approved the appointment of five government-nominated members to the managing committees of cooperative institutions, four of them entitled to vote in board elections. Applied to a board split 13-12, nominated voting members can change who controls the cooperative without another vote of the milk producers themselves. Gandhi, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, alleged on X that the BJP, having lost the producers' vote, changed the rules after the election to stuff in directors and steal the majority — an allegation the Daily Jagran reported alongside criticism from the Congress, the NCP (SP) and a leader of the ruling Shiv Sena. NCP (SP) leader Rohit Pawar urged people to gather outside Gokul Dairy in protest.

Why a dairy board matters this much

Gokul is not a small local union. It collects milk from more than 8,000 village societies in the Kolhapur region, represents several lakh milk-producer farmers — Pawar put the associated societies at 5,400 and farmers at five and a half lakh — and records an annual turnover of roughly Rs 4,000 crore. In western Maharashtra, cooperative dairies and sugar factories are the region's economic engines and its political power bases: whoever controls the board influences milk pricing, procurement and thousands of rural livelihoods. That is why a 13-12 result, and a rule change that follows it, is being fought over at state level. What happens next turns on whether the nominated members are seated on Gokul's committee — and whether the opposition's protest, and any legal challenge, can stop it.
